definition: Negative parallelism is a stylistic device that defines a subject by describing what it is not as well as what it is: "it's not X, it's Y".
details: It has also been called "antithesis", "metalinguistic negation" or "contrastive phrasing". The device has been employed by writers such as Shakespeare ("The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves"; Julius Caesar) or by the football coach Vince Lombardi ("Winning isn’t everything; it’s the only thing"). As a distinct element of style, however, it gained attention only in the 2020s when it became apparent that large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT use negative parallelism inordinately often (about three times more frequently than humans), to the point that such constructions came to be seen as a hallmark of machine-generated text. Although it is not clear why LLMs tend to use negative parallelism to the extent that they do, a few explanations have been suggested: Such constructions are frequent in training data. During reinforcement learning, a phase in LLM training, human reviewers might grade negative parallelism higher because it conveys "the impression of nuance and insight". explainer.lead: Negative parallelism is a rhetorical pattern that defines something by what it is not as well as what it is, as in 'it's not X, it's Y'. It drew attention in the 2020s because large language models such as ChatGPT use it frequently.

tiers.eli5: Instead of just saying what something is, you first say what it isn't, like 'it's not a bug, it's a feature'.
tiers.practitioner: Writers and prompt engineers watch for it because it can read as formulaic when generated at scale; a pitfall is mistaking the pattern for substantive contrast.
tiers.paperLevel: A stylistic device also called antithesis, metalinguistic negation or contrastive phrasing; used by writers such as Shakespeare and coach Vince Lombardi, it has no formal metric and is identified qualitatively.

explainer.example: The line 'The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves' contrasts a false cause with a true one in the same sentence.
